subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: An element has the ground-state electron configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁴. What is the typical charge of the ions of this element in its ionic compounds?
optionWhy: A student who attaches the negative charge of the electron to the number of valence electrons picks this. The atom has six valence electrons but gains only two more, so the charge is −2.
The atom has six valence electrons, 3s²3p⁴. It gains two electrons, giving a valence shell of eight and two more electrons than protons: a charge of −2, as in sulfide.
A student who thinks gaining electrons gives a positive charge picks this. Two electrons are gained, and electrons are negative, so the charge is −2.

A student who takes the charge to equal the number of valence electrons, as for a group 1 or group 2 metal, picks this. A nonmetal with six valence electrons gains two electrons instead of losing six.
questions.explain: The atom has six valence electrons, 3s²3p⁴. It gains two electrons, giving a valence shell of eight and two more electrons than protons: a charge of −2, as in sulfide.
questions.working: The atom has 6 valence electrons (3s²3p⁴). It gains 8 − 6 = 2 electrons to give a valence shell of eight, so the ion has two more electrons than protons: a charge of −2.

questions.q: The complete photoelectron spectrum of an element is shown. What is the typical charge of the ions of this element in its ionic compounds?
optionWhy: A student who thinks every atom completes its octet by gaining electrons picks this: 3 valence electrons, so 5 are gained. A metal atom with three valence electrons loses them instead, forming a +3 ion.
A student who attaches the negative charge of the electron to the number of valence electrons picks this. The three valence electrons are lost, leaving three more protons than electrons: +3.

A student who counts only the electron in the highest-energy subshell (the smallest peak, 3p¹) as a valence electron picks this. The two 3s electrons are also valence electrons, so three electrons are lost.
The five peaks, with relative heights 2, 2, 6, 2 and 1, correspond to 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹. The atom has three valence electrons in its third shell and loses them to form a +3 ion, as aluminum does.
questions.explain: The five peaks, with relative heights 2, 2, 6, 2 and 1, correspond to 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹. The atom has three valence electrons in its third shell and loses them to form a +3 ion, as aluminum does.
questions.working: The peaks correspond to 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹ (relative heights 2, 2, 6, 2, 1), so the atom has 13 electrons and 3 valence electrons (3s²3p¹). Losing the 3 valence electrons gives a charge of +3.

questions.q: The diagram shows a model of the bonding in solid sodium. Which statement about the valence electrons is consistent with the model?
options: They are held in pairs between two neighboring atoms as covalent bonds.
They each stay with the atom they came from and remain part of that atom.
They have been taken by half of the atoms, which become negative ions.
They are spread through the solid and do not belong to any one atom.
optionWhy: A student who thinks metal atoms are joined by covalent bonds picks this. The dots in the model are scattered singly through the solid, not held in pairs between particular atoms.
A student who thinks each electron remains with its own atom picks this. In the model the valence electrons are not attached to particular atoms; they are delocalized through the solid.
A student who thinks a metal contains positive and negative ions picks this. All twelve circles in the model are positive; the negative charge is the delocalized valence electrons.
The model shows the valence electrons scattered throughout the array of positive ions. They are delocalized: not associated with any individual atom.
questions.explain: The model shows the valence electrons scattered throughout the array of positive ions. They are delocalized: not associated with any individual atom.

questions.q: A solid copper wire conducts electricity. Which statement best explains this property in terms of the bonding in copper?
options: Its valence electrons are delocalized and can move through the whole solid.
Its positive ions are loosely held and can move through the whole solid.
Its atoms share electron pairs, which pass from one covalent bond to the next one.
Its positive and negative ions attract each other and pass charge along the wire.
optionWhy: In a metallic solid the valence electrons are delocalized and not associated with any individual atom, so they can move through the solid and carry charge when a voltage is applied.
A student who thinks the ions carry the current in a metal picks this. The positive ions of solid copper stay in their positions; the delocalized electrons move.
A student who thinks metal atoms are joined by covalent bonds picks this. The valence electrons of a metal are not localized in pairs between particular atoms.
A student who thinks a metal contains positive and negative ions picks this. Copper contains positive ions and delocalized electrons, and no negative ions.
questions.explain: In a metallic solid the valence electrons are delocalized and not associated with any individual atom, so they can move through the solid and carry charge when a voltage is applied.

questions.q: The graph shows the potential energy of a pair of H atoms as a function of the distance between their nuclei. Points V, W, X, and Z are marked on the curve. Which point represents the two atoms separated by the equilibrium bond length of H₂?
options: Point V
Point W
Point X
Point Z
optionWhy: A student who thinks bonded atoms sit as close together as possible picks this. At V the nuclei are so close that their repulsion gives the pair a higher potential energy than the separated atoms have; the pair is not at its most stable separation.

The equilibrium bond length is the separation at which the potential energy of the pair is lowest. W is the minimum of the curve, at about 74 pm: at shorter distances repulsion between the nuclei raises the energy, and at longer distances the attraction is weaker.

A student who thinks the bond length is where the potential energy is zero picks this. At X the pair has the same potential energy as the separated atoms; the minimum, at W, lies at a larger separation.

A student who thinks atoms are bonded as soon as they begin to attract picks this. At Z the attraction is weak and the energy is only slightly below zero; the atoms are held most stably at the minimum, W.
questions.explain: The equilibrium bond length is the separation at which the potential energy of the pair is lowest. W is the minimum of the curve, at about 74 pm: at shorter distances repulsion between the nuclei raises the energy, and at longer distances the attraction is weaker.

figure.alt: Graph of Potential energy (kJ/mol), axis marked −500, −400, −300, −200, −100, 0, 100, 200 and 300, with a line at 0, against Distance between nuclei (pm), axis marked 0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250 and 300. One curve falls steeply from high energy at very short distance, crosses 0 near 39 pm, reaches a minimum of about −436 kJ/mol at about 74 pm, then rises gradually toward 0 at large distance. Marked points: V on the steep part at about 34 pm and +200 kJ/mol; X where the curve crosses 0; W at the minimum; Z at about 260 pm and −21 kJ/mol.

questions.q: On a graph of potential energy versus internuclear distance for two atoms that form a diatomic molecule, which quantity is the bond energy of the molecule?
options: The increase in potential energy from the curve's lowest point to complete separation
The value of the potential energy at the minimum, including its negative sign
The energy released as the atoms move from the minimum to a large separation
The value of the potential energy when the two atoms are very far apart
optionWhy: The bond energy is the energy required to separate the atoms: the increase in potential energy from the bottom of the curve (the minimum) to the energy of the atoms far apart. It is a positive quantity, equal to the depth of the minimum below the energy of the separated atoms.

A student who copies the coordinate of the minimum as the bond energy picks this. The bond energy is the energy that must be absorbed, a positive amount equal to the depth of the minimum below the energy of the separated atoms.
A student who thinks breaking a bond releases stored energy picks this. Moving from the minimum to large separation raises the potential energy, so energy is absorbed, not released.

A student who takes the value at one point for the change between two points picks this. The potential energy of separated atoms is the reference level (usually 0); the bond energy is the difference between it and the minimum.
questions.explain: The bond energy is the energy required to separate the atoms: the increase in potential energy from the bottom of the curve (the minimum) to the energy of the atoms far apart. It is a positive quantity, equal to the depth of the minimum below the energy of the separated atoms.
questions.working: Bond energy = energy required to separate the bonded atoms = (potential energy of the separated atoms) − (potential energy at the minimum). With the separated atoms at 0, this is the depth of the minimum, a positive quantity.

questions.q: The diagram represents part of one layer of ions in solid magnesium oxide, MgO. Which statement correctly describes the Mg²⁺ ion labeled X?
options: X is bonded only to the O²⁻ ion that took the two electrons from it
X and one O²⁻ ion form an MgO molecule that is apart from the other ions
X is attracted to each of the O²⁻ ions that surround it in the solid
X is bonded to two O²⁻ ions, one for each unit of its 2+ charge
optionWhy: A student who thinks an ion is bonded only to the ion it exchanged electrons with picks this. Once the ions exist, X attracts every nearby O²⁻ ion according to charge and distance, whichever ion gained its electrons.

A student who thinks ionic solids are made of molecules picks this. X is equally close to several O²⁻ ions, and none of them is set apart with X as a separate unit; MgO is the ratio of ions in the array.

The diagram shows X with O²⁻ ions on every side and no single partner. Each of those oppositely charged neighbors attracts X by Coulombic attraction; the crystal is a continuous array, not a collection of pairs.
A student who thinks an ion forms one bond per unit of charge picks this. The 2+ charge does not limit X to two neighbors; it makes X's attraction to each surrounding O²⁻ ion stronger.
questions.explain: The diagram shows X with O²⁻ ions on every side and no single partner. Each of those oppositely charged neighbors attracts X by Coulombic attraction; the crystal is a continuous array, not a collection of pairs.

questions.q: A crystal of sodium chloride has flat faces and straight edges, and when it is broken, the pieces also have flat faces. Which particulate-level description best explains these observations?
options: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions alternate in a regular pattern that repeats in three dimensions
Each Na⁺ ion and each Cl⁻ ion is itself shaped like a tiny crystal with flat faces
NaCl molecules, each one Na⁺ and one Cl⁻, are stacked side by side in neat rows
Each Na⁺ shares an electron pair with one Cl⁻, which holds the ions at fixed angles
optionWhy: A regular, repeating three-dimensional array of ions produces flat planes of ions throughout the crystal, so the crystal grows and breaks along flat faces. The alternation of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ maximizes attractions and keeps like charges apart.
A student who gives particles the properties of the bulk substance picks this. Ions are not flat-faced; the shape of the crystal comes from the regular arrangement of the ions.
A student who thinks ionic solids are made of molecules picks this. Solid NaCl has no NaCl molecules: each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge in a continuous array.
A student who pictures ionic bonds as shared electron pairs picks this. The ions in NaCl are held by Coulombic attractions between whole ions, which act in all directions; there are no shared pairs.
questions.explain: A regular, repeating three-dimensional array of ions produces flat planes of ions throughout the crystal, so the crystal grows and breaks along flat faces. The alternation of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ maximizes attractions and keeps like charges apart.

questions.q: The diagram represents a particulate model of solid magnesium. Which statement best describes the electrons shown in the model?
options: They are negative ions that hold the positive Mg ions in place
Each one is held in a fixed bond between one particular pair of ions
They are spread among all the ions and are attached to none of them
Each one stays with the magnesium atom that it came from
optionWhy: A student who thinks a metal is held together like an ionic compound picks this. The dots are electrons, not ions; a pure metal contains only one kind of ion, Mg²⁺.
A student who pictures metallic bonding as shared pairs between particular atoms picks this. The electrons are delocalized among all the ions, not localized in bonds between pairs.
The model shows the valence electrons (two from each Mg atom) spread among all the Mg²⁺ ions rather than attached to any one of them: they are delocalized over the whole solid.
A student who pictures a metal as neutral atoms keeping their own electrons picks this. The model shows Mg²⁺ ions with the valence electrons spread among them, not attached to their original atoms.
questions.explain: The model shows the valence electrons (two from each Mg atom) spread among all the Mg²⁺ ions rather than attached to any one of them: they are delocalized over the whole solid.

Key: large circle = Mg²⁺ ion; small dot = electron.

questions.q: A student wants to predict whether atoms of an element Q will substitute for copper atoms in an alloy or will occupy the spaces between copper atoms. Which information about Q and Cu does the student need?
options: The density of solid Q and of solid Cu
The mass of a Q atom and of a Cu atom
The charge on the ion of Q and on the ion of Cu
The atomic radius of a Q atom and of a Cu atom
optionWhy: A student who thinks density shows how large atoms are picks this. Density depends on both the mass of the atoms and how they are packed, so it does not give the atomic radius.

A student who thinks atomic mass decides the type of alloy picks this. Atoms can have very different masses but the same radius (Ag and Au), so mass does not show whether an atom will fit into the spaces.
A student who thinks an alloy is a compound with a fixed formula picks this. An alloy is a mixture of atoms within a metal lattice; no formula needs to balance charges.
Whether the Q atoms fill interstices or substitute depends on how their size compares with that of Cu atoms: significantly smaller atoms fill spaces, and atoms of comparable radius substitute.
questions.explain: Whether the Q atoms fill interstices or substitute depends on how their size compares with that of Cu atoms: significantly smaller atoms fill spaces, and atoms of comparable radius substitute.
questions.working: Interstitial alloys form between atoms of significantly different radii; substitutional alloys form between atoms of comparable radius. The quantities needed are the atomic radii of Q and Cu, to compare their sizes.

questions.q: The Lewis diagram of phosgene, COCl₂, is shown. How many valence electrons does the diagram represent in total?
optionWhy: A student who counts each line as one electron picks this: 4 + 16 = 20. Each line is a shared pair of two electrons, so the bonds hold 8 electrons.

The diagram has four lines (one double bond and two single bonds), which are four shared pairs, or 8 electrons, and eight lone pairs, or 16 electrons: 24 in all. This matches the valence electrons of the atoms, 4 + 6 + 2(7) = 24.
A student who counts each shared pair once for each atom it joins picks this: 2 × 8 + 16 = 32. A shared pair counts toward both atoms' octets, but it is only two electrons in the molecule.

A student who thinks a Lewis diagram accounts for every electron of every atom picks this, adding the atomic numbers: 6 + 8 + 2(17) = 48. The diagram shows only valence electrons: two for each line and two for each pair of dots.
questions.explain: The diagram has four lines (one double bond and two single bonds), which are four shared pairs, or 8 electrons, and eight lone pairs, or 16 electrons: 24 in all. This matches the valence electrons of the atoms, 4 + 6 + 2(7) = 24.
questions.working: Lines: one double bond (2 lines) and two single bonds = 4 bonding pairs = 8 electrons. Dots: 2 lone pairs on O and 3 on each Cl = 8 lone pairs = 16 electrons. Total = 8 + 16 = 24, which matches 4 + 6 + 2(7) = 24.

questions.q: How many valence electrons must be shown in the Lewis diagram of the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
optionWhy: A student who thinks a negative charge means electrons were removed picks this: 30 − 2 = 28. A 2− charge means two extra electrons.
A student who ignores the charge of the ion picks this: 6 + 4(6) = 30. The 2− charge adds two electrons, giving 32.
S and each O have 6 valence electrons, so the atoms supply 6 + 4(6) = 30; the 2− charge means two additional electrons, for a total of 32.
A student who includes every electron of every atom picks this: 16 + 4(8) + 2 = 50. A Lewis diagram shows only valence electrons.
questions.explain: S and each O have 6 valence electrons, so the atoms supply 6 + 4(6) = 30; the 2− charge means two additional electrons, for a total of 32.
questions.working: S (group 16): 6 valence electrons; O: 6 each, 4 × 6 = 24; the 2− charge adds 2 electrons. Total = 6 + 24 + 2 = 32.

questions.q: The diagram shows two equivalent Lewis structures of the nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, joined by a double-headed arrow. Which statement best describes what the pair of structures represents?
options: One ion in which the double bond moves rapidly back and forth between the two N–O positions
One ion in which the two N–O bonds are identical, each between a single and a double bond
A sample in which half of the ions have each of the two bonding arrangements drawn
One ion with a shorter N=O bond and a longer N–O bond, drawn as seen from two opposite sides
optionWhy: A student who thinks a species flips between its resonance structures picks this. The double-headed arrow does not show a change over time; the ion has one unchanging structure with two identical N–O bonds.

The two structures are equivalent, so neither is correct alone; together they describe one ion. Its two N–O bonds are identical, each intermediate in length and strength between an N–O single bond and an N=O double bond, and they stay that way at all times.
A student who thinks each resonance structure pictures some of the particles in a sample picks this. Every nitrite ion is the same, with two identical N–O bonds; no ion has either arrangement alone.

A student who reads one Lewis structure as a literal picture of fixed bonds picks this. The N–O bonds in the nitrite ion are identical, which is why one structure is not enough and resonance must be included.
questions.explain: The two structures are equivalent, so neither is correct alone; together they describe one ion. Its two N–O bonds are identical, each intermediate in length and strength between an N–O single bond and an N=O double bond, and they stay that way at all times.

Right structure: the single and double lines are exchanged, with the lone pairs to match. Caption: Each line is a bonding pair of electrons; each pair of dots is a lone pair.

questions.q: The C–C single bond in ethane, C₂H₆, is 154 pm long, and the C=C double bond in ethene, C₂H₄, is 134 pm long. Two equivalent Lewis structures can be drawn for benzene, C₆H₆, each with alternating C–C and C=C bonds around a ring of six carbon atoms. In an experiment, the six carbon-carbon bond lengths in benzene are measured. Which result does the resonance model of benzene predict?
options: Six equal lengths, each between 134 pm and 154 pm
Three lengths of 134 pm and three of 154 pm in each molecule
Lengths that keep switching between 134 pm and 154 pm
Two sets of lengths, one for each separable form of benzene
optionWhy: Each carbon-carbon position is drawn as a single bond in one structure and a double bond in the other, so the model predicts six identical bonds, shorter than a single bond and longer than a double bond. The measured length of every carbon-carbon bond in benzene is 139 pm.

A student who reads one Lewis structure as a literal picture of fixed single and double bonds picks this. That is the prediction of a single structure without resonance, and it is not what is observed.
A student who thinks a molecule flips back and forth between its resonance structures picks this. The resonance model describes one unchanging structure; the bond lengths do not alternate in time.

A student who thinks resonance structures are different forms of a substance, like isomers, picks this. The two structures have the atoms in the same positions and describe a single kind of molecule, so there are no separate forms to measure.
questions.explain: Each carbon-carbon position is drawn as a single bond in one structure and a double bond in the other, so the model predicts six identical bonds, shorter than a single bond and longer than a double bond. The measured length of every carbon-carbon bond in benzene is 139 pm.
questions.working: Two equivalent structures exist, so resonance must be included: each carbon-carbon position is single in one structure and double in the other. All six bonds are therefore identical and intermediate between a single bond (154 pm) and a double bond (134 pm). (The measured value is 139 pm.)

questions.q: VSEPR theory predicts that the two C=O bonds in a CO₂ molecule lie on opposite sides of the C atom, 180° apart. On what basis does VSEPR theory make this prediction?
options: Repulsion between the two O atoms, which are farthest apart on opposite sides of C
The polarity of the two C=O bonds, which holds the two bonds on opposite sides of C
Repulsion between the electron domains on C, which get as far apart as possible
The Lewis diagram of CO₂, which is written with all three of its atoms in a straight line
optionWhy: A student who thinks shape is set by repulsion between the outer atoms picks this. VSEPR theory treats the electron domains around the central atom as repelling one another; the positions of the O atoms follow from where the domains point.

A student who thinks bond polarity decides shape picks this. VSEPR predicts the same 180° arrangement for any central atom with two domains and no lone pairs, polar bonds or not; the polarity of the bonds plays no part in the prediction.

VSEPR theory rests on Coulombic repulsion between electrons. The C atom in CO₂ has two electron domains (two double bonds) and no lone pairs; two domains are farthest apart on opposite sides of the atom, so the O atoms at the ends of those domains are 180° apart.

A student who reads shape from the layout of a Lewis diagram picks this. A Lewis diagram can be drawn at any angle on paper; the 180° angle comes from applying VSEPR to the two electron domains around C.
questions.explain: VSEPR theory rests on Coulombic repulsion between electrons. The C atom in CO₂ has two electron domains (two double bonds) and no lone pairs; two domains are farthest apart on opposite sides of the atom, so the O atoms at the ends of those domains are 180° apart.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the carbon–carbon bond in ethyne, H–C≡C–H, with the carbon–carbon bond in ethane, H₃C–CH₃?
options: The C≡C bond is stronger, as more electron pairs are shared between the two C nuclei
The C≡C bond is weaker, as each of its two pi bonds is weaker than a sigma bond
The two bonds are equally strong, as each joins the same two kinds of atom
The C≡C bond is three times as strong, as it consists of three identical C–C bonds
optionWhy: Bond order is 3 in ethyne and 1 in ethane. Three shared pairs (one sigma and two pi bonds) hold the two C nuclei together more strongly than one, so the C≡C bond has the greater bond energy.

A student who thinks adding pi bonds makes a bond weaker picks this. Each pi bond is weaker than the sigma bond, but the pi bonds add to the sigma bond, so the triple bond is the stronger bond (839 vs 347 kJ/mol).
A student who thinks bond energy depends only on the two elements picks this. Bonds between the same two atoms differ greatly with bond order: C≡C needs much more energy to break than C–C.

A student who thinks the bonds within a multiple bond are identical picks this. A triple bond is one sigma and two weaker pi bonds, so its bond energy (839 kJ/mol) is much less than three times that of C–C (347 kJ/mol).
questions.explain: Bond order is 3 in ethyne and 1 in ethane. Three shared pairs (one sigma and two pi bonds) hold the two C nuclei together more strongly than one, so the C≡C bond has the greater bond energy.

questions.q: The diagram represents a small part of a molecular solid made of nonpolar X₂ molecules. Which statement correctly describes what the solid lines and the dashed lines represent?
options: Solid lines are covalent bonds within molecules; dashed lines are attractions between molecules.
Solid lines are intermolecular forces within molecules; dashed lines are covalent bonds between molecules.
Solid lines and dashed lines are covalent bonds of two lengths, linking the atoms into one network.
Solid lines are covalent bonds within molecules; dashed lines mark spacing between molecules that do not attract.
optionWhy: Each pair of circles joined by a solid line is one X₂ molecule, held together by a covalent bond. The dashed lines join atoms of different molecules and represent the intermolecular attractions (here London dispersion forces) that hold the molecules in the solid.

A student who confuses 'inter' with 'intra' picks this, placing intermolecular forces inside the molecule and covalent bonds between molecules. The covalent bond is the link within each X₂ molecule; the intermolecular forces act between molecules.

A student who thinks the attractions between molecules are covalent bonds picks this. Only the solid line within each X₂ molecule is a covalent bond; no electrons are shared between neighboring molecules.

A student who thinks nonpolar molecules do not attract one another picks this. Nonpolar molecules attract by London dispersion forces, and these attractions are what hold the X₂ molecules together in the solid.
questions.explain: Each pair of circles joined by a solid line is one X₂ molecule, held together by a covalent bond. The dashed lines join atoms of different molecules and represent the intermolecular attractions (here London dispersion forces) that hold the molecules in the solid.

questions.q: The diagram represents potassium chloride, KCl, as a solid and as a liquid, each connected to a conductivity tester. Which statement correctly describes what the diagram shows?
options: The same ions are present in the solid and in the liquid, but they move from place to place only in the liquid.
Electrons are released from the ions when the solid melts, and these electrons move through the liquid to light the bulb.
The solid is made of KCl molecules, which the tester cannot detect, and these break up into ions only in the liquid.
Charges from the tester pass through the gaps between the ions, and these gaps are wide enough only in the liquid.
optionWhy: Both parts of the diagram show K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In the solid the ions are in a regular, fixed arrangement and the bulb is off; in the liquid the arrows show the ions moving, and the bulb is lit. The current is carried by the mobile ions.
A student who thinks only electrons can carry a current picks this. The diagram shows no free electrons: the moving particles in the liquid are the K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions themselves.
A student who thinks an ionic compound consists of molecules picks this. The diagram shows separate K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in the solid, each surrounded by ions of opposite charge, not KCl molecules.

A student who thinks the charges in a current come only from the battery and pass through gaps in the material picks this. The arrows in the diagram are on the ions: the K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions themselves move and carry the current in the liquid.
questions.explain: Both parts of the diagram show K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In the solid the ions are in a regular, fixed arrangement and the bulb is off; in the liquid the arrows show the ions moving, and the bulb is lit. The current is carried by the mobile ions.

Left, labeled Solid KCl and Bulb off: twelve ions in a regular array of three rows of four, K⁺ and Cl⁻ alternating, no arrows; the bulb is dark. Right, labeled Liquid KCl and Bulb lit: ten ions, five K⁺ and five Cl⁻, in an irregular arrangement, each with a small arrow pointing in a different direction; the bulb is drawn with rays. Key: small circle with + = K⁺; larger circle with − = Cl⁻; arrow = ion moving.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the changes in bonds and attractions that occur as solid sodium chloride, NaCl(s), dissolves in water?
options: Ionic bonds between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ break, and ion-dipole attractions to water form
Attractions between NaCl molecules break, and the molecules spread out among water molecules
Covalent bonds in water molecules break, and new NaOH and HCl molecules then form
All bonds in NaCl break, and separate Na and Cl atoms spread out among water molecules
optionWhy: Solid NaCl consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by ionic bonds. As it dissolves, these ionic bonds are broken and the separated ions are attracted to the polar water molecules: Na⁺ to the O ends and Cl⁻ to the H ends.

A student who thinks ionic compounds are made of molecules picks this. Solid NaCl contains no NaCl molecules; it is a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, and these ions separate from one another as it dissolves.

A student who thinks dissolving a salt is a reaction with water that forms new compounds picks this. The water molecules stay intact; the ions separate from the lattice and are surrounded by water molecules, and evaporation recovers NaCl.

A student who thinks a dissolving substance breaks up into separate atoms picks this. The particles in solution are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, the same charged particles that make up the solid, not neutral atoms.
questions.explain: Solid NaCl consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by ionic bonds. As it dissolves, these ionic bonds are broken and the separated ions are attracted to the polar water molecules: Na⁺ to the O ends and Cl⁻ to the H ends.
questions.working: No calculation. NaCl(s) is a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. On dissolving, the ionic bonds between the ions are broken and each ion becomes surrounded by water molecules held by ion-dipole interactions; the water molecules stay intact.

questions.q: Which of the following processes involves the breaking of covalent bonds?
options: Melting a sample of ice at 0°C
Boiling a sample of ethanol
Dissolving table sugar in water
Decomposing hydrogen peroxide
optionWhy: A student who thinks hydrogen bonds are the O–H bonds inside a water molecule picks this. Melting overcomes some hydrogen bonds between separate water molecules; the covalent O–H bonds within each molecule stay intact.
A student who thinks boiling breaks the covalent bonds within molecules picks this. Boiling separates whole ethanol molecules from one another; the vapor still consists of ethanol molecules.
A student who thinks a dissolving substance breaks up into its atoms picks this. Sugar dissolves as intact molecules surrounded by water molecules; no covalent bonds within the sugar molecules break.

In 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂ the atoms are rearranged into new substances: O–O and O–H bonds in H₂O₂ are broken and new bonds form in H₂O and O₂. This is a chemical process; the other three involve only changes in intermolecular interactions.
questions.explain: In 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂ the atoms are rearranged into new substances: O–O and O–H bonds in H₂O₂ are broken and new bonds form in H₂O and O₂. This is a chemical process; the other three involve only changes in intermolecular interactions.
questions.working: No calculation. Melting ice and boiling ethanol are phase changes: only intermolecular attractions change. Dissolving sugar separates intact sugar molecules. Decomposing hydrogen peroxide, 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂, breaks O–O and O–H bonds and forms new O–H and O=O bonds.
